ru_2018 = launches[(launches.state_code=='RU') & (launches.launch_year==2018)].shape[0]

us_peak = launches[launches.state_code=='US'].groupby('launch_year').size()
print(f"US peak: {us_peak.idxmax()} with {us_peak.max()} launches")
us_2018 = launches[(launches.state_code=='US') & (launches.launch_year==2018)].shape[0]
print(f"US 2018: {us_2018}")

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the great inversion
raw_evidence.content: If you froze the world in 1985 and asked who would dominate the launch business in 2018, almost no one would have answered 'a private American company and the People's Republic of China.' The Soviet Union was running 90+ launches per year; the US was the only Western challenger; China had launched its first satellite only 15 years earlier and was still launching only a handful. The dataset captures this inversion in a single 60-year arc: the dominant agency of the 1970s–80s (Soviet RVSN, 1,528 launches) had been retired by 1991, and the dominant agency of 2018 (SpaceX) had not yet existed in 1985. This is the strongest narrative tension in the data.

sources.title: The space race is dominated by new contenders — The Economist
facts: Article frames the launch market as inverted from Cold War expectation

raw_evidence.label: The new contenders: SpaceX, China, and the startup wave
raw_evidence.content: Three big shifts reshape the 2010s: (1) China (state, but a new contender by global cadence) ramps from a few launches per year in the 1990s to surpassing the United States in some years after 2015. (2) SpaceX, founded 2002 by Elon Musk, conducts its first orbital launch in 2008 (Falcon 1) and grows to over 20 launches in 2018 alone — more than any other single agency that year. The first Falcon 9 first-stage land-back in December 2015 inaugurated reusable orbital launch. (3) A wave of startups (Rocket Lab, Blue Origin, Virgin Orbit, etc.) targets the small-satellite market, driven by cheap CubeSats and university demand. The Economist's 'new contenders' framing maps to all three.

facts: China conducted 39 orbital launches in 2018, surpassing the US that year

raw_evidence.label: Soviet peak vs. Russian collapse vs. China's rise
raw_evidence.content: The Soviet Union's launch peak was 108 in 1982 — a cadence the United States never matched in any single year (the US peak was 77 in 1966). By 2018 Russia, the inheritor of Soviet capability, conducted only 10 launches: barely 9% of its 1982 high. China's trajectory ran the other way, from 5 launches in 1990 to 28 in 2018.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_03: Soviet peak vs current state ---
print("=== ana_03 ===")
sov_peak = launches[launches.state_code=='SU'].groupby('launch_year').size()
print(f"Soviet peak year: {sov_peak.idxmax()} with {sov_peak.max()} launches")
print(f"Soviet final year: 1991 with {launches[(launches.state_code=='SU') & (launches.launch_year==1991)].shape[0]}")
ru_2018 = launches[(launches.state_code=='RU') & (launches.launch_year==2018)].shape[0]
print(f"Russia 2018: {ru_2018}")
us_peak = launches[launches.state_code=='US'].groupby('launch_year').size()
print(f"US peak: {us_peak.idxmax()} with {us_peak.max()} launches")
us_2018 = launches[(launches.state_code=='US') & (launches.launch_year==2018)].shape[0]
print(f"US 2018: {us_2018}")
cn_2018 = launches[(launches.state_code=='CN') & (launches.launch_year==2018)].shape[0]
print(f"China 2018: {cn_2018}")
cn_1990 = launches[(launches.state_code=='CN') & (launches.launch_year==1990)].shape[0]
print(f"China 1990: {cn_1990}")
raw_evidence.output:
Soviet peak year: 1982 with 108 launches
Soviet final year: 1991 with 61
Russia 2018: 10
US peak: 1966 with 77 launches
US 2018: 27
China 2018: 28
China 1990: 5

raw_evidence.label: Top providers in 2018
raw_evidence.content: The 2018 leaderboard is unrecognisable from 1985's. China's state code (CN) is first with 28 launches. SpaceX is second with 17 — more than the entire Russian state apparatus that year (9). Arianespace had 6, the original Soviet successor RU had 9, and Rocket Lab's first commercial year produced 1 launch from Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_07 ===")
top_2018 = launches[launches.launch_year==2018].agency.value_counts().head(15)
print(top_2018)
raw_evidence.output:
CN 28
SPX 17
RU 9
AE 6
ULAL 5
IN 4
MHI 3
ULAB 3
J 2
EUROK 1
OSC 1
RLABU 1

raw_evidence.label: 2018 cadence by bloc — China overtakes
raw_evidence.content: Within 2018's 80 launches (data through October), China leads with 28, the United States is second with 27, the 'Other' bloc combined for 15, and Russia trails at 10. It is the first year in the dataset where neither superpower's successor leads.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_18 ===")
b2018 = launches[launches.launch_year == 2018].bloc.value_counts()
print(f"2018 (partial through Oct): total {b2018.sum()}")
for b, c in b2018.items():
    print(f"{b}: {c}")
raw_evidence.output:
2018 (partial through Oct): total 80
China: 28
United States: 27
Other: 15
USSR/Russia: 10

raw_evidence.label: The Cold War space race (1957–1991)
raw_evidence.content: From Sputnik in October 1957 until the dissolution of the Soviet Union at the end of 1991, orbital launch was almost entirely a contest between two states. The USSR launched at a faster cadence than the United States for most of the period, peaking near 100 launches per year in the early 1980s, while the US peaked around 60–70 in the late 1960s. Together the two superpowers accounted for the overwhelming majority of all attempts; commercial launches in the modern sense did not exist. After 1991 the Soviet inventory was inherited largely by Russia (RU) and, for a time, Ukraine, with state agencies such as RVSN and UNKS giving way to Roscosmos.

raw_evidence.label: The 1990s lull and commercial slow-down
raw_evidence.content: After the Soviet collapse, total launches fell sharply: Russian funding for both civilian (Roscosmos) and military space dried up, and the US government cut back on military launches as Cold War procurement wound down. The 1990s and early 2000s were the lowest cadence years since the early 1960s — typically 60–80 launches per year worldwide. Commercial activity did exist (Arianespace, started 1980; Lockheed-Martin and Boeing's Atlas/Delta lines) but failed to replace state demand. Many observers in the early 2000s wrote about a 'space recession.'

raw_evidence.label: The new contenders: SpaceX, China, and the startup wave
raw_evidence.content: Three big shifts reshape the 2010s: (1) China (state, but a new contender by global cadence) ramps from a few launches per year in the 1990s to surpassing the United States in some years after 2015. (2) SpaceX, founded 2002 by Elon Musk, conducts its first orbital launch in 2008 (Falcon 1) and grows to over 20 launches in 2018 alone — more than any other single agency that year. The first Falcon 9 first-stage land-back in December 2015 inaugurated reusable orbital launch. (3) A wave of startups (Rocket Lab, Blue Origin, Virgin Orbit, etc.) targets the small-satellite market, driven by cheap CubeSats and university demand. The Economist's 'new contenders' framing maps to all three.

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the great inversion
raw_evidence.content: If you froze the world in 1985 and asked who would dominate the launch business in 2018, almost no one would have answered 'a private American company and the People's Republic of China.' The Soviet Union was running 90+ launches per year; the US was the only Western challenger; China had launched its first satellite only 15 years earlier and was still launching only a handful. The dataset captures this inversion in a single 60-year arc: the dominant agency of the 1970s–80s (Soviet RVSN, 1,528 launches) had been retired by 1991, and the dominant agency of 2018 (SpaceX) had not yet existed in 1985. This is the strongest narrative tension in the data.

raw_evidence.label: Yearly launches by bloc — the great inversion
raw_evidence.content: Splitting launches by bloc shows the Cold War duopoly turning inside out. The USSR led every year from 1967 to 1991, peaking at 108 launches in 1982 — more than four times its US rival that year. Russia's inheritance of the Soviet program then declined, falling from 91 in 1991 to just 10 in 2018. Meanwhile China rose from a single launch in 1970 to 28 in 2018, surpassing both Russia and the United States in cadence. By 2018 the order is China (28), the United States (27), the 'Other' bloc (15) — and Russia, the original space leader, last at 10.

total = launches.agency_type.value_counts()
print(f"TOTAL by agency_type:")
print(total)
print(f"% breakdown: state={total['state']/total.sum()*100:.1f}%, private={total['private']/total.sum()*100:.1f}%, startup={total['startup']/total.sum()*100:.1f}%")

# yearly by agency_type
yearly_type = launches.groupby(['launch_year', 'agency_type']).size().unstack(fill_value=0).reset_index()
print(f"\nYEARLY by agency_type:")
print(yearly_type.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: The new contenders: SpaceX, China, and the startup wave
raw_evidence.content: Three big shifts reshape the 2010s: (1) China (state, but a new contender by global cadence) ramps from a few launches per year in the 1990s to surpassing the United States in some years after 2015. (2) SpaceX, founded 2002 by Elon Musk, conducts its first orbital launch in 2008 (Falcon 1) and grows to over 20 launches in 2018 alone — more than any other single agency that year. The first Falcon 9 first-stage land-back in December 2015 inaugurated reusable orbital launch. (3) A wave of startups (Rocket Lab, Blue Origin, Virgin Orbit, etc.) targets the small-satellite market, driven by cheap CubeSats and university demand. The Economist's 'new contenders' framing maps to all three.

raw_evidence.label: Failure rates and learning curves
raw_evidence.content: Orbital launch failures were common in the early years — roughly one in three launches failed during 1957–1962 — and dropped sharply as vehicles matured, settling around 5–8% from the 1990s onward. Failures cluster around new vehicle introductions: the maiden flight of any new launcher carries roughly 30–50% risk historically. Reusable boosters introduce a new class of failure (recovery failure) that does not affect the primary mission outcome; the JSR data uses the binary success (O) / failure (F) classification at the orbital-insertion level.

raw_evidence.label: Failure rate by agency type
raw_evidence.content: Private firms have the lowest failure rate at 2.6% (23/880) — they entered late, with mature vehicle designs and proven engineering. State agencies sit at 6.6% (314/4,776), pulled up by the Cold War's experimental years. Startups, the smallest cohort, have the highest rate at 7.1% (5/70) — a reminder that new vehicles still fail at roughly the historical maiden-flight rate.

# --- ana_11: Failure rate by agency_type ---
print("=== ana_11 ===")
ft = launches.groupby('agency_type').agg(total=('category','size'), failures=('failed','sum'))
ft['fail_pct'] = ft.failures / ft.total * 100
print(ft.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Failure rates
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: 53.8% → 3% over six decades is striking. Note the counter-intuitive ordering: private (2.6%) < state (6.6%) < startup (7.1%).

raw_evidence.label: Failure rates and learning curves
raw_evidence.content: Orbital launch failures were common in the early years — roughly one in three launches failed during 1957–1962 — and dropped sharply as vehicles matured, settling around 5–8% from the 1990s onward. Failures cluster around new vehicle introductions: the maiden flight of any new launcher carries roughly 30–50% risk historically. Reusable boosters introduce a new class of failure (recovery failure) that does not affect the primary mission outcome; the JSR data uses the binary success (O) / failure (F) classification at the orbital-insertion level.

sentences.context: A geography that has barely moved
sentences.summary: det_08: Major launch sites and their geography. Source: Spaceport — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceport) Facts: Equatorial launch sites give a velocity boost from Earth's rotation; Baikonur, Plesetsk, Cape Canaveral, Vandenberg, Jiuquan, and Kourou are the main historical orbital launch sites

raw_evidence.label: Major launch sites and their geography
raw_evidence.content: Launch sites concentrate in a handful of high-latitude or equatorial locations chosen for safety (downrange ocean) and orbital efficiency (closer to the equator = bigger payload boost from Earth's rotation). Soviet launches went mostly from Baikonur (Kazakhstan, 46°N) and Plesetsk (62°N); American launches from Cape Canaveral (28°N) and Vandenberg (35°N); China from Jiuquan (41°N) and Xichang (28°N); ESA from Kourou, French Guiana (5°N — the most equatorial major spaceport, giving European launchers a payload bonus). The agencies CSV's lat/lng columns let us map every launch provider, though many entries are missing coordinates.

raw_evidence.label: Synthesised launch-site coordinates (reference layer)
raw_evidence.content: The agencies CSV's lat/long fields are mostly missing or set to '-' (the dataset's null sentinel). This is reference geography, not a per-launch coordinate join: individual launches in the data do not carry site coordinates.

    ("Xichang",                 "Sichuan, CN",         28.246, 102.027, "CN"),
    ("Taiyuan",                 "Shanxi, CN",          38.849, 111.608, "CN"),
    ("Wenchang",                "Hainan, CN",          19.614, 110.951, "CN"),
    ("Tanegashima",             "Japan",               30.401, 130.969, "J"),
    ("Uchinoura",               "Japan",               31.251, 131.082, "J"),
    ("Satish Dhawan",           "Sriharikota, India",  13.733,  80.235, "IN"),

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters in 2018
raw_evidence.content: By 2018 the launch market had become a leading indicator for how space power was being redistributed. The number of payloads in orbit was about to explode (Starlink alone would launch its first batch in May 2019, scaling to 60 satellites per launch). National security analysts were debating whether the United States could rely on commercial launch for sensitive payloads, while emerging space agencies (India's ISRO, Israel, Iran, North Korea) were proving that orbital access was no longer the exclusive privilege of the two original superpowers. The Economist's headline reflects this: the 'race' was becoming a market, and the players were no longer who you would have guessed in 1990.

sources.title: The space race is dominated by new contenders — The Economist
facts: Article published October 2018 framed launch trends as a redistribution of space power
Highlighted China's rise and SpaceX's commercial dominance

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the great inversion
raw_evidence.content: If you froze the world in 1985 and asked who would dominate the launch business in 2018, almost no one would have answered 'a private American company and the People's Republic of China.' The Soviet Union was running 90+ launches per year; the US was the only Western challenger; China had launched its first satellite only 15 years earlier and was still launching only a handful. The dataset captures this inversion in a single 60-year arc: the dominant agency of the 1970s–80s (Soviet RVSN, 1,528 launches) had been retired by 1991, and the dominant agency of 2018 (SpaceX) had not yet existed in 1985. This is the strongest narrative tension in the data.

raw_evidence.label: Why this matters in 2018
raw_evidence.content: By 2018 the launch market had become a leading indicator for how space power was being redistributed. The number of payloads in orbit was about to explode (Starlink alone would launch its first batch in May 2019, scaling to 60 satellites per launch). National security analysts were debating whether the United States could rely on commercial launch for sensitive payloads, while emerging space agencies (India's ISRO, Israel, Iran, North Korea) were proving that orbital access was no longer the exclusive privilege of the two original superpowers. The Economist's headline reflects this: the 'race' was becoming a market, and the players were no longer who you would have guessed in 1990.

sources.title: The space race is dominated by new contenders — The Economist
facts: Article published October 2018 framed launch trends as a redistribution of space power
Highlighted China's rise and SpaceX's commercial dominance

raw_evidence.label: Interpretive hook — the great inversion
raw_evidence.content: If you froze the world in 1985 and asked who would dominate the launch business in 2018, almost no one would have answered 'a private American company and the People's Republic of China.' The Soviet Union was running 90+ launches per year; the US was the only Western challenger; China had launched its first satellite only 15 years earlier and was still launching only a handful. The dataset captures this inversion in a single 60-year arc: the dominant agency of the 1970s–80s (Soviet RVSN, 1,528 launches) had been retired by 1991, and the dominant agency of 2018 (SpaceX) had not yet existed in 1985. This is the strongest narrative tension in the data.
